Poodle skirt
POO-dul skurt
noun (Silent Generation slang)
American fashion word of the 1950s for a wide, full-circle felt skirt decorated with an appliqué poodle, often with a rhinestone collar and a looping leash. The felt circle skirt is commonly traced to California fashion of the late 1940s; the poodle became its most famous decoration, and by the mid-1950s the skirt, worn over petticoats with bobby socks and saddle shoes, was the very picture of the teenage girl at a sock hop.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

For a girl in 1955, nothing said party like a poodle skirt: a great circle of pink or gray felt that swirled out when she spun on the dance floor, a little felt poodle stitched near the hem, and two or three crinoline petticoats underneath to make it stand out. Mothers sewed them at the kitchen table; girls added their own touches. It was a cheerful, girlish fashion, and on the whole a modest one, falling well below the knee. Scripture has room for that kind of delight. The prophet compares the joy of salvation to dressing up: "as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels" (Isa 61:10). Yet the same Scripture keeps clothing in its place. Women are to "adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety" (1Ti 2:9), and the truest ornament is "the hidden man of the heart" (1Pe 3:4). Proverbs adds a word every teenage girl needs: "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised" (Pro 31:30). And Isaiah’s verse holds the best news of all: "he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness" (Isa 61:10). A grandmother who still has her poodle skirt in a cedar chest can show it to her granddaughter and tell her both stories: how much fun it was to twirl, and how much better it is to be clothed by Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation fashion word (American, 1950s) for the full felt circle skirt with an appliquéd poodle, worn over petticoats at the sock hop — cheerful and modest, and a picture of the robe of righteousness (Isa 61:10).

expand to see more

POODLE SKIRT, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) A wide, full-circle felt skirt decorated with an appliqué poodle, usually worn over crinoline petticoats. "Mom stayed up till midnight sewing the poodle on my skirt for the dance."

Webster (1828) — SKIRT, noun 1. The lower and loose part of a coat or other garment; the part below the waist; as the skirt of a coat or mantle. 4. A woman’s garment like a petticoat.

Decode for families: a twirl in a felt skirt was innocent fun; the lasting garment is the robe of righteousness.

Key Scripture

Isa 61:10 — "I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels."

1Ti 2:9 — "In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;"

1Pe 3:4 — "But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price."

Pro 31:30 — "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised."

Modern Corruption

A cheerful, generally modest fashion with nothing to correct in itself; the only caution is the old one against making clothing the measure of a girl’s worth.

expand to see more

There is no sin in a poodle skirt. It was a homemade, girlish fashion, usually sewn by mothers and worn to chaperoned dances, and by any standard it was modest. Delight in pretty clothes is not vanity in itself; Scripture uses a bride’s adornment as a picture of salvation (Isa 61:10).

The caution is about where a girl’s heart rests. A teenage world that ranks girls by the newest skirt teaches them to seek favour, which is deceitful (Pro 31:30). A Christian family can enjoy the old fashion and still teach that the hidden ornament of a meek and quiet spirit is what God calls of great price (1Pe 3:4).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

German Pudelhund (splash-dog, a water retriever) → English poodle + Old Norse skyrta (shirt) → English skirt → poodle skirt (1950s).

expand to see more

German Pudelhund — a water dog, from Low German pudeln, to splash

Old Norse skyrta — shirt, tunic; English skirt, the lower garment

Late 1940s: the felt circle skirt in California fashion

1950s: the appliqué poodle; petticoats, bobby socks, saddle shoes

Usage

""I still have my pink poodle skirt in the cedar chest. It swirled out like a parasol when I spun.""

"I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God (Isa 61:10)."
